title: Fabric Streaming Analytics: Hot and Cold Paths from One Event Stream
purpose: Trace how a single stream of events fans out from Eventstream into a hot operational path (Eventhouse KQL, Activator alerting) and a cold historical path (OneLake availability, lakehouse, Power BI), and how the two paths converge for cross-engine reporting.
accessibleSummary: An architecture flow starting at event sources feeding into Eventstream, which routes and shapes events with built-in stream-processing operators. From there the flow splits: the hot path lands events in an Eventhouse KQL database for indexed, low-latency query and native anomaly detection, feeding Activator rules that fire alerts and automated actions, and Real-Time Dashboards for live monitoring. The cold path uses OneLake availability to write the same KQL table data into Delta format with adaptive batching, making it queryable by lakehouse, warehouse, Spark, and Power BI Direct Lake without any copy. A warning node covers the DDL operations blocked while OneLake availability is enabled, and a feedback edge shows Activator triggering Fabric jobs that write back into the lakehouse cold path.
longDescription: This is an architecture flow showing a genuinely branching topology: one event stream serves two different latency requirements without being duplicated by hand. Event sources feed Eventstream, a no-code pipeline that filters, cleanses, deduplicates, and routes events to multiple destinations simultaneously. The hot path sends events into an Eventhouse KQL database, which auto-organizes records by arrival time for fast indexed queries and offers native in-place anomaly detection; Activator watches KQL, event, or Power BI conditions and fires notifications, automations, or Fabric job/Spark/Dataflow executions when thresholds or patterns are met, and Real-Time Dashboards expose the same hot data for live operational monitoring. The cold path is not a separate ingestion pipeline — it is OneLake availability, a feature that adaptively batches the same KQL table data into Delta Parquet files with no additional storage charge, making it directly queryable by lakehouse, warehouse, Spark notebooks, and Power BI Direct Lake with zero data movement. A feedback edge captures Activator's ability to trigger Fabric jobs or Spark jobs that write further processed output back into the lakehouse, closing the loop between the automated-action path and the historical store. A warning node names the specific DDL operations that are blocked while OneLake availability is active on a table.

nodes.label: Event sources
nodes.summary: Kafka, Kinesis, Pub/Sub, MQTT, CDC feeds, and other streaming producers.
nodes.detail: Streaming analytics starts with producers emitting events continuously: message brokers like Apache Kafka, AWS Kinesis, and Google Cloud Pub/Sub, MQTT-based device telemetry, and CDC feeds from operational databases surfaced through Real-Time hub. Real-Time hub also catalogs Fabric workspace item events and Microsoft-managed sources tenant-wide.
nodes.whyItMatters: The architecture's entire hot/cold split downstream depends on these sources being genuinely event-driven; a batch-oriented source is usually better served by a scheduled pipeline instead of this streaming path.

evidence.note: Real-Time hub functions as an organization-wide catalog of data in motion, surfacing active data streams, Microsoft-managed sources (including CDC feeds from Azure SQL DB, Cosmos DB, and PostgreSQL), and Fabric workspace item events.

Eventstreams provide a no-code pipeline for collecting, transforming, and routing high-volume real-time data to multiple destinations simultaneously. Supported sources include Apache Kafka, AWS Kinesis, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, MQTT, and a Real-Time Weather connector.

inputs: A continuous producer: Kafka topic, MQTT broker, Kinesis stream, CDC-enabled database, or Microsoft-managed source
processing: Producer emits events continuously rather than in scheduled batches
Events reach Fabric through a source connector, optionally over a private network via a Streaming virtual network data gateway
outputs: A raw event stream ready for Eventstream ingestion
drill.example: IoT sensors on delivery vehicles publish location and status events to an MQTT broker continuously throughout each trip.
controls: Choice of source connector and authentication method (SASL_SSL, mTLS, custom CA)
failureModes: Routing a fundamentally batch-shaped source (e.g. a nightly file drop) through this streaming path when a scheduled pipeline would be simpler and cheaper

nodes.label: Eventstream
nodes.summary: No-code ingestion, shaping, and routing to multiple destinations simultaneously.
nodes.detail: Eventstreams provide a no-code pipeline for collecting, transforming, and routing high-volume real-time data to multiple destinations at once. Built-in stream-processing operators include filtering, cleansing, windowed aggregations, deduplication, and content-based routing, and derived eventstreams can package these transformations as reusable, shareable outputs.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the single point where one incoming event gets shaped once and fanned out to both the hot and cold destinations, avoiding two separate, potentially inconsistent ingestion pipelines for the same data.

evidence.note: Eventstreams provide a no-code pipeline for collecting, transforming, and routing high-volume real-time data to multiple destinations simultaneously.

Eventstreams expose built-in stream processing operators — filtering, cleansing, windowed aggregations, deduplication, and content-based routing — so data can be shaped before landing at a destination.

inputs: Raw events from one or more configured sources
processing: Apply filter, cleanse, dedup, windowed-aggregation, and routing operators as configured
Fan out the shaped stream to multiple destinations concurrently (Eventhouse, Lakehouse, Activator, custom endpoints)
outputs: A shaped, routed event stream landing simultaneously at hot-path and cold-path destinations
drill.example: A vehicle-telemetry eventstream deduplicates retried messages and routes speeding events to an Eventhouse KQL database while also routing the full unfiltered stream to a lakehouse for archival.
controls: Which stream-processing operators are applied and in what order
Destination routing rules (content-based or blanket fan-out)
failureModes: Under Workspace Outbound Access Protection, cross-workspace or external destinations are blocked by default unless a data connection rule explicitly permits them

nodes.label: Eventhouse KQL database (hot path)
nodes.summary: Indexed, low-latency store organized by arrival time, with native anomaly detection.
nodes.detail: Eventhouses automatically organize ingested records by arrival time, enabling fast, indexed queries over structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data at any scale. Eventhouse includes native anomaly detection that evaluates live time-series and event datasets in place, without requiring data copies or exports, reducing detection latency.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the operational query surface: the arrival-time indexing and in-place anomaly detection are what make sub-second dashboards and alerting possible directly against streaming data, without waiting for a batch job to materialize results.

evidence.note: An Eventhouse is a workspace-level container that can host multiple KQL databases, allowing them to share underlying capacity and resources. KQL database storage is split into a premium cache tier holding the hot dataset and a standard tier holding the full retention window.

Eventhouses automatically organize ingested records by arrival time, enabling fast, indexed queries over structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data at any scale. Eventhouse includes native anomaly detection that evaluates live time-series and event datasets in place.

processing: Ingest and auto-organize records by arrival time into the premium cache tier
Serve KQL, T-SQL, and KQL queryset queries against the hot cache
Run native anomaly detection in place against live time-series data
outputs: Sub-second query results and anomaly signals for dashboards and Activator rules
drill.example: A logistics Eventhouse ingests vehicle location pings, and a live dashboard queries the last 10 minutes of speed readings per vehicle directly from the hot cache tier.
controls: Caching policy governing the hot cache window (shorter windows reduce premium-tier spend)
Retention policy governing total queryable history in the standard tier
failureModes: When query demand exceeds capacity, throttling escalates through proactive, reactive, and extreme-reactive stages, with the last carrying a real risk of data loss after a holding period

nodes.label: Activator
nodes.summary: Monitors live conditions and fires notifications, automations, or Fabric job executions.
nodes.detail: Activator monitors data flowing through Real-Time hub, KQL queries, or Power BI reports and fires automated actions — notifications, Fabric pipeline/Spark job/Dataflow executions, User Data Function calls, or Power Automate workflows — when threshold, pattern, or KQL-defined conditions are met. Fabric events and Azure Blob Storage events exposed in Real-Time hub can trigger Activator rules to start Spark jobs or Dataflows with no polling schedule required.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is what turns a detected condition into an actual response — the difference between a dashboard someone has to watch and a system that reacts on its own the moment a threshold is crossed.

evidence.note: Activator monitors data flowing through Real-Time hub, KQL queries, or Power BI reports and fires automated actions — such as sending notifications, launching Fabric pipeline or Spark job or Dataflow executions, calling User Data Functions, or triggering Power Automate workflows — when threshold, pattern, or KQL-defined conditions are met.

Fabric events and Azure Blob Storage events exposed in Real-Time hub can trigger Activator rules to start Spark jobs or Dataflows, enabling fully event-driven orchestration that requires no polling schedule.

inputs: A defined rule condition: threshold, pattern, or KQL query against Eventhouse, Power BI, or Real-Time hub data
processing: Continuously evaluate the condition against live data
On match, fire the configured action: notification, Fabric job, Spark job, Dataflow, User Data Function, or Power Automate flow
outputs: A triggered action: an alert delivered, or a downstream job/pipeline launched
drill.example: An Activator rule watches the Eventhouse for any vehicle reporting zero GPS signal for over 5 minutes and fires both a Teams notification to dispatch and a Spark job that flags the vehicle in the lakehouse for follow-up.
controls: Action target and, under Workspace Outbound Access Protection, whether that target is same-workspace or requires an explicit data connection rule
failureModes: Under OAP, Power Automate triggered from Activator is blocked outright with no current override, and email notifications default to same-tenant recipients only

nodes.label: OneLake availability (cold path)
nodes.summary: Adaptive batching writes the same KQL table data into Delta Parquet, no separate pipeline.
nodes.detail: Enabling OneLake availability exposes KQL table data in Delta Lake format, directly queryable by other Fabric engines — Power BI Direct Lake, Warehouse, Lakehouse, and Spark notebooks — with no data movement or additional storage charge beyond standard OneLake storage. An adaptive batching mechanism delays writes until enough data accumulates for optimally sized Parquet files (typically 200-256 MB), with a default max delay of up to 3 hours, configurable down to 5 minutes.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is what makes the cold path free of a second ingestion pipeline: it's the same KQL table, just made visible to every other Fabric engine as Delta, which is the structural reason hot and cold paths stay consistent rather than drifting apart.

evidence.note: Enabling OneLake availability exposes KQL table data in Delta Lake format, making it directly queryable by other Fabric engines — including Power BI Direct Lake mode, Warehouse, Lakehouse, and Spark notebooks — without any data movement or copy. There is no additional storage charge beyond standard OneLake storage.

When OneLake availability is active, an adaptive batching mechanism delays writes to OneLake until enough data accumulates to produce optimally-sized Parquet files (typically 200-256 MB). The default maximum delay is up to 3 hours; it can be lowered to as little as 5 minutes via the mirroring policy, though smaller delays risk producing many small files.

inputs: KQL table data already ingested into the Eventhouse hot path
processing: Adaptive batching accumulates enough rows to target a 200-256 MB Parquet file
Writes the batch to OneLake as Delta once the size target or max delay is reached
outputs: The same table data, now queryable as Delta by lakehouse, warehouse, Spark, and Power BI Direct Lake with zero copy
drill.example: A vehicle-telemetry KQL table with OneLake availability enabled writes new Delta files roughly every hour under normal load; a lakehouse notebook joins this cold-path data with warehouse trip dimensions for a weekly utilization report.
controls: Mirroring policy delay setting (5 minutes to 3 hours) trading file size against freshness
Database-level vs table-level OneLake availability scope, with optional backfill
failureModes: Lowering the delay too aggressively produces many small files that degrade downstream query performance — see the warning node for the specific DDL constraints this feature also imposes

nodes.label: Trap: DDL operations blocked under OneLake availability
nodes.summary: Renaming, retyping, RLS, and row deletes are blocked while OneLake availability is active on a table.
nodes.detail: While OneLake availability is enabled on a table, certain DDL operations are blocked: renaming the table, changing a column's data type, applying row-level security, and deleting or purging rows. These operations require temporarily disabling OneLake availability, and re-enabling it afterward triggers a full historic backfill.
nodes.whyItMatters: A team that enables OneLake availability before schema and security decisions are stable discovers routine schema changes now require a disable/backfill cycle — turning what should be a quick DDL statement into an operational event.

evidence.note: While OneLake availability is enabled on a table, certain DDL operations are blocked: renaming the table, changing a column's data type, applying row-level security, and deleting or purging rows. These operations require temporarily disabling OneLake availability; re-enabling it triggers a full historic backfill.

inputs: A KQL table with OneLake availability enabled, needing a schema or security change
processing: Attempted rename, type change, RLS application, or row purge fails while availability is active
Team must temporarily disable OneLake availability to make the change
Re-enabling availability triggers a full backfill of historic data, not an incremental resume
outputs: Either an avoided problem (schema finalized before enabling availability) or an unplanned backfill event
drill.example: A team enables OneLake availability on a fast-moving telemetry table early, then needs to apply row-level security for a new compliance requirement; the change requires disabling availability and re-enabling it, triggering a full historic backfill that consumes unplanned capacity.
controls: Stabilize schema and security decisions before enabling OneLake availability on a table
Plan any necessary future DDL changes around the disable/backfill cost
failureModes: Discovering the DDL restriction only when an urgent security or schema fix is needed, forcing an unplanned backfill under time pressure

nodes.label: Lakehouse / Warehouse / Power BI (cold-path consumers)
nodes.summary: Cross-engine reporting and joins over the OneLake-available Delta data.
nodes.detail: Because OneLake availability exposes the KQL data as Delta with no data movement, lakehouse notebooks, warehouse T-SQL, Spark, and Power BI Direct Lake models can all query or join it like any other OneLake table. A proven pattern is combining a lakehouse and warehouse in one workspace: land and transform in the lakehouse, then surface curated datasets through the warehouse for SQL-centric reporting teams.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is where the cold path pays off: historical, cross-domain analysis that would be awkward or expensive to run directly against the hot KQL cache instead runs against the same data using each team's preferred engine.

evidence.note: A proven pattern is to combine both item types in one workspace: land and transform raw data in a lakehouse with Spark, then surface curated datasets through a warehouse for SQL-centric reporting teams.

inputs: Delta-form KQL table data made available via OneLake availability
processing: Lakehouse notebooks join it with other Delta tables via Spark
Warehouse T-SQL queries it via cross-database queries or shortcuts
Power BI Direct Lake models read it directly with no import refresh
outputs: Historical, cross-domain reports and joins that would be impractical against the hot KQL cache alone
drill.example: A quarterly utilization report joins the cold-path vehicle telemetry Delta table with warehouse-held maintenance records and customer contract dimensions, something the hot KQL path wasn't designed to serve.
controls: Which engine (Spark, T-SQL, Direct Lake) is the right fit per consuming team's skills
failureModes: Routing what is actually a daily-freshness batch requirement through this streaming path when a plain lakehouse or warehouse pipeline would be simpler and cheaper

edges.label: same table, adaptively batched to Delta

walkthrough.title: 1. Events originate from continuous producers
walkthrough.explanation: Kafka, MQTT, CDC feeds, and other streaming sources feed the pattern; a batch-shaped source belongs on a scheduled pipeline instead.

walkthrough.title: 2. One shaping and routing point
walkthrough.explanation: Eventstream filters, dedupes, and fans the shaped stream out to both the hot and cold destinations at once, so there's only one ingestion path to maintain.

walkthrough.title: 3. Hot path: indexed for low-latency query
walkthrough.explanation: The Eventhouse KQL database auto-organizes by arrival time and runs anomaly detection in place, powering sub-second dashboards and alert conditions.

walkthrough.title: 4. Detected conditions become actions
walkthrough.explanation: Activator turns a threshold or pattern match into a real response: a notification, or a downstream Fabric/Spark job launched with no polling schedule.

walkthrough.title: 5. Cold path: the same table, made Delta
walkthrough.explanation: OneLake availability isn't a second pipeline — it adaptively batches the same KQL table into Delta Parquet, visible to every other Fabric engine at no extra storage cost.

walkthrough.title: 6. Warning: schema changes get expensive once availability is on
walkthrough.explanation: Renaming, retyping, RLS, or row deletes are blocked while OneLake availability is active — stabilize the schema first, or accept a full backfill later.

walkthrough.title: 7. Historical and cross-domain analysis converges here
walkthrough.explanation: Lakehouse, warehouse, and Power BI Direct Lake all query the same cold-path data, and Activator's triggered jobs can write further processed output back into this same layer.
